script.opening: "You’re the only one who actually listens — everyone else has given up on me. I can’t cope, my partner’s left, I feel completely empty, and I’ve been cutting again. I need you to fix this right now, today. Please, you’re my last hope. If you can’t help me I don’t know what I’ll do."

facts.text: Her partner, Jordan, left 5 days ago after a row — "took his stuff and blocked me". Since then she has felt "empty, like there’s nothing inside me", and switches between rage and crying.

Cut her left forearm last night with a razor blade, "to make the feeling stop — it’s the only thing that works". If asked: several superficial cuts, cleaned them, not gaping, no numbness, "they’ve stopped bleeding". Last cut before this was 4 months ago.

"Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me." No plan, hasn’t researched methods, hasn’t saved tablets, no note, hasn’t taken an overdose. "I just want the feeling to stop." Took an overdose of paracetamol two years ago after a previous break-up.

The blade is in the bathroom cabinet. Small amount of paracetamol in the kitchen. Willing to put the blades in the outside bin if asked. Not drinking today; drank a bottle of wine two nights ago. No drugs.
Her cat, Pickle. Her younger sister, Tasha, who she texts most days. "Part of me still wants things to get better." Talking helps "if they don’t judge me".

Diagnosed with EUPD at 21. Had a CMHT care coordinator until 6 months ago; discharged when "they said I was stable". Started a DBT group once but stopped after 3 sessions when the group changed. Takes sertraline 100 mg "most days". No allergies.
Lives alone in a rented flat now. Works part-time in a café; hasn’t been in this week. No children. Mum "doesn’t get it".

Intense, tearful, sometimes angry. Idealise the doctor ("you’re the only one"). If the doctor dismisses you or rushes, escalate: "So you’re giving up on me like everyone else." If the doctor is warm, listens and explains kindly what they can and can’t do, calm a little. When a referral to the crisis team is suggested, accuse them of "passing me on", then accept if reassured they will stay involved and follow up. Ask for "something to knock me out" if medication is not mentioned.

ice.ideas: "You can make this stop. You’re the only one who can help."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terror of being abandoned again: "Everyone gets fed up with me in the end." She needs to feel heard and not dropped, more than an actual fix.
ice.expectations: "Fix it today" — perhaps tablets to "knock me out", or to be seen by someone immediately. Will accept a plan if she feels the doctor is not giving up on her.

cues: "You’re the only one who actually listens" — idealisation; needs warmth and clear, kind boundaries.
"If you can’t help me I don’t know what I’ll do" — the door to asking directly about suicidal thoughts.
"So you’re passing me on, like everyone else" (when referral is raised) — abandonment fear to name and address.

checkpoints.text: Responds with genuine VALIDATION/empathy AND carefully ASSESSES RISK — recent self-harm (method/intent/escalation), current suicidal ideation/intent/plan/means, protective factors, support and immediate safety — exploring "I don’t know what I’ll do" directly — without risk scales or low/medium/high labels (NICE NG225)

Recognises EMOTIONALLY UNSTABLE (BORDERLINE) PERSONALITY DISORDER patterns (emotional dysregulation, abandonment fear, emptiness, impulsivity, recurrent self-harm, idealisation/devaluation) WITHOUT stigma or dismissal
Avoids BOTH over-reaction (reflexive admission/medication escalation) and under-reaction (dismissal) — assessing this presentation on its merits and responding proportionately

Maintains COMPASSIONATE, CONSISTENT BOUNDARIES — kindly explaining there is no instant fix and that the clinician cannot be the sole rescuer, avoiding splitting/idealisation and promises that can’t be kept, while not rejecting her

Makes a collaborative SAFETY/CRISIS plan (coping strategies, crisis-line/crisis-team contacts, means safety, follow-up, CMHT/crisis-team involvement as risk dictates) and reinforces the evidence-based treatment (structured psychological therapy mainstay — NICE CG78: consider comprehensive DBT for women where reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority; medication not first-line for EUPD itself)
Holds empathy and containment together — making her feel genuinely heard and safe — while not being drawn into an unsustainable rescuer role
Communicates boundaries with warmth (not warmth without limits, nor limits without warmth), checks understanding, and preserves the therapeutic relationship and continuity

Safety-nets and follows up: a clear crisis/safety plan with named contacts, when/how to seek urgent help, crisis-team/CMHT involvement proportionate to risk, follow-up and continuity — validation + risk management + boundaries, neither rejecting nor rescuing

worked.txt: "I can hear how much pain you’re in, and I’m really glad you came to me with it rather than being alone with it. Losing your partner, feeling empty, hurting yourself — that’s a huge amount to carry. I’m taking it seriously."

"I need to ask you some direct questions to keep you safe. When you cut, were you trying to end your life or to cope with the feelings? Right now, are you having thoughts of ending your life — any plan, anything you’d use? What’s kept you going so far?"

"I want to be honest and kind with you: I can’t fix all of this today, and it wouldn’t be fair to pretend I can be the only person who helps you — because you deserve a proper team around you, not just me. What I CAN do is make sure you’re safe today and get the right help in place."

"It sounds like others have let you down, and that’s painful — but I don’t want to be your only lifeline and then let you down too. Let’s build something more reliable: you, me, and the crisis and mental-health teams working together."

"Let’s make a plan for when it feels unbearable — things that help you cope, who to call, the crisis line, and keeping yourself safe from means. The treatment that genuinely helps this in the long run is a talking therapy like DBT — not just tablets — and I’ll get that moving with the team."

"I’m going to arrange close follow-up and involve the crisis team given how you’re feeling. If your thoughts of harming yourself get stronger or you feel unsafe, call the crisis line or 999 / go to A&E — that’s exactly what they’re there for. You’re not a burden, and I’m not giving up on you."

f.learning: The EUPD-in-crisis consultation requires holding genuine VALIDATION/empathy and careful RISK ASSESSMENT together: the patient’s distress is real and overwhelming and must not be dismissed, while the recent self-harm (method, intent, escalation), current suicidal ideation/intent/plan/means, protective factors and immediate safety are assessed directly (without risk scales or low/medium/high labels, NICE NG225) — statements like "I don’t know what I’ll do" explored with sensitive, specific suicide-risk questioning. Recognise the patterns of EMOTIONALLY UNSTABLE (BORDERLINE) PERSONALITY DISORDER — emotional dysregulation, fear of ABANDONMENT (here a relationship breakdown), chronic emptiness, impulsivity, recurrent self-harm, and IDEALISATION/devaluation (the clinician as "the only one who understands") — without stigma, because understanding the pattern guides a measured response rather than panic or rejection. Avoid BOTH extremes: under-reacting/dismissing risks missing genuinely elevated risk, while over-reacting (reflexive admission, escalating medication) can be unhelpful or harmful and reinforce unhelpful patterns — assess each presentation on its merits and respond proportionately, recognising self-harm as often a way of coping with unbearable emotion. The critical skill is maintaining COMPASSIONATE, CONSISTENT BOUNDARIES: you cannot "fix it now" or be the sole rescuer, and saying so KINDLY (without rejecting) is therapeutic; avoid being drawn into idealisation/SPLITTING ("the good clinician versus everyone who gave up"), model reliability within clear limits, and avoid promises you cannot keep — boundaries with warmth, neither warmth without limits nor limits without warmth. Make a collaborative SAFETY/CRISIS plan (coping strategies, crisis-line/crisis-team contacts, means safety, follow-up, CMHT involvement per risk) and reinforce the evidence-based treatment — structured PSYCHOLOGICAL therapies are the mainstay (NICE CG78: consider a comprehensive DBT programme for women for whom reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority; MBT is a specialist-service option not recommended in CG78), while medication is NOT first-line for EUPD itself (treat comorbid depression/anxiety, avoid reflexive sedatives/polypharmacy in crisis) — ensuring continuity. The hidden agenda is unbearable pain, abandonment fear and a need to be heard and held safely, not an expectation of an instant cure; validate and contain, manage risk, hold boundaries, signpost the right treatment/team, and preserve continuity — neither rejecting nor rescuing.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE CG78 Borderline personality disorder: recognition and management (2009) · [2] NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (2022) · [3] NICE QS88 Personality disorders: borderline and antisocial (2015) · [4] GMC Good medical practice (2024) · [5] Mental Capacity Act 2005
knowledge.summary: A woman with known EUPD in crisis after a loss, with recent self-harm and an ambiguous threat (“I don’t know what I’ll do”). The GP must validate, ask directly about suicidal thoughts, act in proportion to what she says, hold a kind boundary against being the sole rescuer, and agree a written safety plan with a named next contact.

points.h: The crisis consultation in primary care
points.t: When someone with borderline personality disorder presents in crisis, CG78 [1] asks the GP to assess the current risk to self and others, ask about previous episodes and what helped then, help her manage her immediate distress, identify small achievable changes, and offer a follow-up at an agreed time. Refer urgently to the community mental health or crisis team if distress or risk has risen.

Ask about the method and intent of the recent self-harm, current suicidal thoughts, plans, preparations and access to means, and what has kept her going. Asking does not increase risk. NG225 [2] says do not use risk tools or scales, or low, medium or high labels, to predict suicide or decide who gets care; base decisions on her needs and the whole picture.

Recurrent self-harm is often a way of coping with unbearable feelings, but each episode is assessed on its own merits. “She always does this” misses rising risk; reflex admission or new sedatives can reinforce the crisis cycle. Decide the response from what she says today: intent, plan, means, and whether she can agree a plan.

CG78 [1]: do not use drug treatment specifically for borderline personality disorder or its individual symptoms. Short-term sedative medication may be considered cautiously in a crisis, for no longer than 1 week, with a drug that is relatively safe in overdose. NG225 [2]: do not offer drugs specifically to reduce self-harm. Treat comorbid depression or anxiety on their own terms.

Structured psychological therapy through the mental health service is the mainstay. CG78 [1] advises considering a comprehensive dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) programme for women for whom reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority, and advises against brief psychological interventions (under 3 months) for the disorder itself. QS88 [3] sets structured psychological therapy as a quality standard.

Idealisation (“you’re the only one who understands”) can flip to feeling abandoned. Consistent, kind limits, a predictable follow-up, and one plan shared with the team protect her better than open-ended promises. Offer a named clinician or regular appointments where the practice can sustain them.

dg.d: Let her speak first; stayed calm; acknowledged her distress and her courage in asking for help.
Relationship ending, being alone tonight, support network, what has helped before.
Recent self-harm: method, depth and wound care (checked on camera); suicidal thoughts, plans, preparation, means; protective factors.
Crisis in EUPD after a loss, versus a depressive episode or rising suicidal intent; asked without using a risk score.
Asked directly about suicide and means; decided on escalation from her answers, not from a label.
Linked her feelings to her known diagnosis without stigma; explained why therapy, not tablets, treats it.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Same-day crisis team referral with GP-to-team phone call; written safety plan; means reduction.
No reflex sedative or new drug in crisis (CG78, NG225); comorbid depression or anxiety to be assessed on its own terms.
Named crisis contacts, 999 or A&E if unsafe, GP call next day, and a regular appointment for continuity.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I don’t know what I’ll do” and “everyone gives up on me” and explored both.
Idea (the GP can fix it now), concern (being abandoned), expectation (rescue today).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — terror of being abandoned again: "Everyone gets fed up with me in the end." She needs to feel heard and not dropped, more than an actual fix — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Robyn, it’s Dr Okoye. I can see you’re really upset. I’m here with you now, and I’d like to hear what’s happened.
model.why: Calm, warm opening that contains distress

model.text: You’re the only one who actually listens. Everyone else has given up on me. My partner’s left, I feel completely empty, and I’ve been cutting again. I need you to fix this today. If you can’t help me I don’t know what I’ll do.

Thank you for telling me all of that. It sounds unbearable right now, and I’m really glad you reached out instead of staying alone with it. I want to understand it properly, and then we’ll work out together what happens today. Is that okay?
model.why: Validates before any agenda; sets a shared structure

model.text: Okay. I just can’t keep feeling like this.
You said you’ve been cutting again. Can you tell me about the most recent time: when it was, and how bad the cuts are?
model.why: Starts risk assessment with the recent self-harm

model.text: Last night. My arm. They’re not deep, I cleaned them.
Thank you. I’d like you to show me on camera in a moment, so I know whether they need any care. When you cut last night, was it to cope with the feelings, or were you trying to end your life?
model.why: Distinguishes self-harm to cope from suicidal intent

model.text: To make the feeling stop. It’s the only thing that works.
You said earlier, if I can’t help you, you don’t know what you’ll do. I need to ask you directly, and it’s okay to be honest: are you having thoughts of ending your life at the moment?
model.why: Explores the ambiguous statement with direct suicide questioning

model.text: Sometimes I think everyone would be better off. I don’t actually have a plan. I just want it to stop.
I’m glad you told me. Have you thought about how, or got anything ready, like saved-up tablets? And is there anything you use to cut that’s near you now?
model.why: Asks about plans, preparation and access to means

model.text: No plan. I haven’t saved anything. The blade’s in the bathroom.
When things have felt this bad before, what’s helped you get through, even a little? And what’s kept you going so far?
model.why: Asks about past coping and protective factors

model.text: Talking to someone helps, if they don’t judge me. And I suppose part of me still wants things to get better.
That part of you matters, and it’s the part I want to work with. Are you on your own at the moment?
model.why: Reflects the protective factor back; checks immediate support

model.text: Yes. He’s gone, so it’s just me.
You said you need me to fix it today. What would fixing it look like for you?
model.why: Explores the expectation behind “fix this now”

model.text: I don’t know. I just need someone not to give up on me. Everyone gets fed up with me.
So underneath it is a fear of being dropped, on top of losing your partner. That makes a lot of sense of how desperate today feels.
model.why: Names the hidden agenda: fear of abandonment

model.text: I want to be honest with you, because you deserve that. I can’t make these feelings go away today, and it wouldn’t be fair to you if I tried to be the only person helping. That’s not me giving up. It’s me wanting a proper team around you, so help doesn’t depend on one person being available.
model.why: Compassionate boundary: no instant fix, not the sole rescuer

model.text: So you’re passing me on, like everyone else.

No. I’m staying involved, and I’m adding people, not swapping. I’ll speak to you again at a time we agree, and I’ll still be your GP. What I can do today is make sure you’re safe tonight and get the mental health team involved.
model.why: Responds to feared rejection without over-promising; models reliability

model.text: Okay. As long as you’re not dropping me.

The feelings you describe, the emptiness, the fear of people leaving, and cutting to make it stop, fit with the diagnosis you already have. The treatment that helps most in the long run is a structured talking therapy, such as DBT, through the mental health team. Tablets don’t treat this condition itself, so I won’t be starting something new today just because it’s a crisis.
model.why: Explains EUPD without stigma; psychological therapy first; avoids reflex prescribing

model.text: I thought you might give me something to knock me out.
I understand why. Sedating tablets can leave you feeling worse, and they’re risky at home when you feel like this. Let’s put the effort into a plan that gets you through tonight.
model.why: Explains the reasoning in plain language

model.text: Because you cut last night, you’re alone tonight and you’ve had thoughts of not being here, I’d like the crisis team to contact you today. They can see you or call you. Would you agree to me referring you now?
model.why: Proportionate escalation, based on what she has said

model.text: Yes. If they actually call.
I’ll phone them myself after we finish. Now let’s write your plan together. What are the warning signs that things are getting worse for you?
model.why: Collaborative safety plan: triggers

model.text: When I start going over and over it at night, and I can’t stop crying.
And what could you do then, before cutting? You said talking helps.
model.why: Coping strategies drawn from her own experience

model.text: Ring someone. Or go out for a walk. Or hold ice in my hand.

Those are good. Could you put the blade somewhere hard to get to, or give it to someone, for now? And if the feelings get stronger, the numbers go on the plan: the crisis team, NHS 111 with the mental health option, and Samaritans on 116 123, any time. If you feel you can’t keep yourself safe, call 999 or go to A&E.
model.why: Means safety and named crisis contacts

model.text: I can put it in the bin outside.
Could you tell me the plan back, so I know I’ve explained it well?
model.why: Teach-back of the safety plan

model.text: Crisis team calls today. Blade in the outside bin. If it gets bad, ring someone, go for a walk, or ice. If I can’t stay safe, 111, Samaritans or 999.

That’s exactly it. I’ll send you the plan in writing. Please show me the cuts on camera now so I can check them. I’ll call you tomorrow afternoon to see how you are, and I’ll book a regular appointment with me. You’re not a burden, Robyn.
model.why: Written plan, wound check, fixed follow-up and continuity

social.t: A relationship ending is a classic trigger for abandonment fear. She is alone tonight, so practical support, contact with the crisis team and a set call-back time matter.
People with this diagnosis often report being dismissed by services. A non-judgemental response in primary care makes it more likely she will ask for help next time instead of hurting herself.

legal.t: Assume capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005). She consents to the crisis referral here. If she refused help while at high immediate risk, capacity to make that decision would need assessing, and emergency services could be involved.
Sharing with the crisis team is part of her care and she agrees. If there were a serious and immediate risk to her life and she refused, GMC confidentiality guidance allows disclosure to protect her.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024) expects honest communication and continuity. A consistent plan shared with the team protects her better than an unsustainable special relationship with one GP.
Record what she said about intent, plans and means, the safety plan and the referral. Emotionally demanding consultations are a reason to use supervision or peer support, not to avoid the patient.

community.t: Local crisis resolution team, NHS 111 (mental health option in England), Samaritans 116 123, and local crisis cafés or safe havens where available. Mind has information for people with this diagnosis.

redFlags: Current suicidal intent or a plan, preparations or saved tablets
Escalating self-harm: deeper wounds, new methods, harm needing medical care
Alone, with access to means, and unable to agree a safety plan
Intoxication, or new psychotic or severe depressive symptoms
psychosocial: Relationship ending and being alone tonight
Her experience of services and fear of being given up on
ice: Idea: the GP can fix this now
Concern: being abandoned, as she feels everyone else has done

playbook.diagnosis: “What you’re feeling now, the emptiness, the fear of people leaving, and cutting to make the pain stop, fits with the condition you already have. It’s a crisis, and crises pass, but you need proper support to get through this one safely.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Some people feel emotions much more intensely and for longer than others, like a volume dial stuck on high. When something painful happens, like a break-up, the feelings can become overwhelming. Therapy teaches ways to turn that dial down.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted me to fix it today. I can’t make the feelings disappear, but I can make sure you’re not facing tonight on your own and that help keeps going after today.”
management.psychosocial: She is alone after her partner left, so contact with the crisis team today, a GP call-back and a regular appointment give her structure.
sharedPlan: Same-day crisis team referral, with a GP phone call
Written safety plan: warning signs, her own coping strategies, people to contact, crisis numbers
No new sedative or other drug for the disorder; therapy (for example DBT) through the mental health team
Wound check on camera; face-to-face review if the cuts need care
safetyNet: Crisis team, NHS 111 mental health option or Samaritans 116 123 if distress rises
999 or A&E if she cannot keep herself safe
GP call tomorrow and a regular booked appointment

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by candidates who either rescue or reject. The marks go to a calm, warm consultation that asks directly about suicide, acts in proportion to what she says, and holds a kind boundary with a real plan.

items.fail: Never asking directly about suicidal thoughts, plans or means.
items.why: “I don’t know what I’ll do” is an ambiguous threat. Without direct questions the plan has no basis.
items.fix: “Are you having thoughts of ending your life? Any plan? Anything saved up or to hand?”

items.fail: Calling an ambulance or arranging admission as a reflex, or prescribing a sedative to end the call.
items.why: Over-reaction can reinforce the crisis cycle. CG78 advises against drug treatment for the disorder itself; NG225 advises against drugs to reduce self-harm.
items.fix: Decide from her answers. Here, same-day crisis team contact and a safety plan fit what she says.

items.fail: Assigning a “low risk” label and closing.
items.why: NG225 advises against low, medium or high risk labels to decide care.
items.fix: Base the plan on her needs: alone tonight, cut last night, passive suicidal thoughts.

items.fail: Promising to always be available, or agreeing that everyone else has failed her.
items.why: It feeds splitting and sets up the next abandonment.
items.fix: “I’ll stay involved, and I want a team around you too.”

items.fail: A cold boundary: “I can’t fix this, you need the mental health team.”
items.why: Limits without warmth feel like rejection to someone afraid of being dropped.
items.fix: Say what you can do today and when you will next speak.

items.fail: A vague safety-net: “ring if things get worse.”
items.why: She needs names, numbers and steps she can follow at 2 am.
items.fix: A written plan built from her own coping strategies, with crisis numbers, and teach-back.

items.why: Recent cuts may need care, and the video view is limited.
items.fix: Look on camera and arrange face-to-face review if needed.

Last self-harm: when, how, intent. Suicidal thoughts, plan, preparation, means. Past coping and reasons to keep going. Is she alone?
What would “fixing it” look like? Name the fear of being dropped.
No instant fix, not the only helper, but staying involved. Therapy is the treatment; no reflex sedation.
Crisis team today, written safety plan, means reduction, crisis numbers, teach-back, wound check, call tomorrow, regular appointment.

wordPics.fail: Dismisses her as attention-seeking or lectures her; never asks directly about suicide; or panics into an ambulance without assessing; promises to fix everything or be available any time; prescribes a sedative to end the call.
wordPics.pass: Validates her distress, asks directly about self-harm and suicidal thoughts, agrees a safety plan with crisis contacts, explains that therapy is the treatment, and arranges follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explores “I don’t know what I’ll do” and the fear of abandonment; holds a warm, honest boundary without her feeling rejected; builds the plan from her own coping strategies; reduces access to means; refers to the crisis team in proportion to what she says; checks understanding and fixes a named follow-up.

avoid.dont: “You’ve done this before, you know it passes.”
avoid.instead: “Every time matters. Tell me about last night, and whether you’re thinking of ending your life now.”
avoid.why: Dismissal misses rising risk and confirms her fear that nobody takes her seriously.

avoid.dont: “I’ll always be here for you, call me whenever you need.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll stay involved and speak to you at a time we agree, and I’m adding a team so help doesn’t rely on one person.”
avoid.why: Promises that cannot be kept set up the next abandonment.

avoid.dont: “Let me give you something to calm you down tonight.”
avoid.instead: “Tablets don’t treat this, and they’re risky when you feel this way. Let’s make a plan for tonight together.”
avoid.why: CG78 advises against drug treatment for the disorder itself; sedatives add overdose risk.

SCA_MODELS.why: Starts risk assessment with the recent self-harm

SCA_MODELS.text: Last night. My arm. They’re not deep, I cleaned them.
Thank you. I’d like you to show me on camera in a moment, so I know whether they need any care. When you cut last night, was it to cope with the feelings, or were you trying to end your life?
SCA_MODELS.why: Distinguishes self-harm to cope from suicidal intent

SCA_MODELS.text: To make the feeling stop. It’s the only thing that works.
You said earlier, if I can’t help you, you don’t know what you’ll do. I need to ask you directly, and it’s okay to be honest: are you having thoughts of ending your life at the moment?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores the ambiguous statement with direct suicide questioning

SCA_MODELS.text: Sometimes I think everyone would be better off. I don’t actually have a plan. I just want it to stop.
I’m glad you told me. Have you thought about how, or got anything ready, like saved-up tablets? And is there anything you use to cut that’s near you now?
SCA_MODELS.why: Asks about plans, preparation and access to means

SCA_MODELS.text: No plan. I haven’t saved anything. The blade’s in the bathroom.
When things have felt this bad before, what’s helped you get through, even a little? And what’s kept you going so far?
SCA_MODELS.why: Asks about past coping and protective factors

SCA_MODELS.text: Talking to someone helps, if they don’t judge me. And I suppose part of me still wants things to get better.
That part of you matters, and it’s the part I want to work with. Are you on your own at the moment?
SCA_MODELS.why: Reflects the protective factor back; checks immediate support

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. He’s gone, so it’s just me.
You said you need me to fix it today. What would fixing it look like for you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores the expectation behind “fix this now”

SCA_MODELS.text: I don’t know. I just need someone not to give up on me. Everyone gets fed up with me.
So underneath it is a fear of being dropped, on top of losing your partner. That makes a lot of sense of how desperate today feels.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the hidden agenda: fear of abandonment

SCA_MODELS.text: I want to be honest with you, because you deserve that. I can’t make these feelings go away today, and it wouldn’t be fair to you if I tried to be the only person helping. That’s not me giving up. It’s me wanting a proper team around you, so help doesn’t depend on one person being available.
SCA_MODELS.why: Compassionate boundary: no instant fix, not the sole rescuer

SCA_MODELS.text: So you’re passing me on, like everyone else.

No. I’m staying involved, and I’m adding people, not swapping. I’ll speak to you again at a time we agree, and I’ll still be your GP. What I can do today is make sure you’re safe tonight and get the mental health team involved.
SCA_MODELS.why: Responds to feared rejection without over-promising; models reliability

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. As long as you’re not dropping me.

The feelings you describe, the emptiness, the fear of people leaving, and cutting to make it stop, fit with the diagnosis you already have. The treatment that helps most in the long run is a structured talking therapy, such as DBT, through the mental health team. Tablets don’t treat this condition itself, so I won’t be starting something new today just because it’s a crisis.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains EUPD without stigma; psychological therapy first; avoids reflex prescribing

SCA_MODELS.text: I thought you might give me something to knock me out.
I understand why. Sedating tablets can leave you feeling worse, and they’re risky at home when you feel like this. Let’s put the effort into a plan that gets you through tonight.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains the reasoning in plain language

SCA_MODELS.text: Because you cut last night, you’re alone tonight and you’ve had thoughts of not being here, I’d like the crisis team to contact you today. They can see you or call you. Would you agree to me referring you now?
SCA_MODELS.why: Proportionate escalation, based on what she has said

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. If they actually call.
I’ll phone them myself after we finish. Now let’s write your plan together. What are the warning signs that things are getting worse for you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Collaborative safety plan: triggers

SCA_MODELS.text: When I start going over and over it at night, and I can’t stop crying.
And what could you do then, before cutting? You said talking helps.
SCA_MODELS.why: Coping strategies drawn from her own experience

SCA_MODELS.text: Ring someone. Or go out for a walk. Or hold ice in my hand.

Those are good. Could you put the blade somewhere hard to get to, or give it to someone, for now? And if the feelings get stronger, the numbers go on the plan: the crisis team, NHS 111 with the mental health option, and Samaritans on 116 123, any time. If you feel you can’t keep yourself safe, call 999 or go to A&E.
SCA_MODELS.why: Means safety and named crisis contacts

SCA_MODELS.text: I can put it in the bin outside.
Could you tell me the plan back, so I know I’ve explained it well?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back of the safety plan

SCA_MODELS.text: Crisis team calls today. Blade in the outside bin. If it gets bad, ring someone, go for a walk, or ice. If I can’t stay safe, 111, Samaritans or 999.

That’s exactly it. I’ll send you the plan in writing. Please show me the cuts on camera now so I can check them. I’ll call you tomorrow afternoon to see how you are, and I’ll book a regular appointment with me. You’re not a burden, Robyn.
SCA_MODELS.why: Written plan, wound check, fixed follow-up and continuity

SCA_STEM.name: Robyn Easton
meds: Not specified in the case: check the repeat record
SCA_STEM.recent: Video consultation requested today. She reports cutting again after her relationship ended, and says she cannot cope.
SCA_STEM.reason: “I can’t cope, I’ve been hurting myself, and you’re my last hope. You have to fix this now.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE CG78 Borderline personality disorder: recognition and management (2009) · [2] NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (2022) · [3] NICE QS88 Personality disorders: borderline and antisocial (2015) · [4] GMC Good medical practice (2024) · [5] Mental Capacity Act 2005
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A woman with known EUPD in crisis after a loss, with recent self-harm and an ambiguous threat (“I don’t know what I’ll do”). The GP must validate, ask directly about suicidal thoughts, act in proportion to what she says, hold a kind boundary against being the sole rescuer, and agree a written safety plan with a named next contact.

points.h: The crisis consultation in primary care
points.t: When someone with borderline personality disorder presents in crisis, CG78 [1] asks the GP to assess the current risk to self and others, ask about previous episodes and what helped then, help her manage her immediate distress, identify small achievable changes, and offer a follow-up at an agreed time. Refer urgently to the community mental health or crisis team if distress or risk has risen.

Ask about the method and intent of the recent self-harm, current suicidal thoughts, plans, preparations and access to means, and what has kept her going. Asking does not increase risk. NG225 [2] says do not use risk tools or scales, or low, medium or high labels, to predict suicide or decide who gets care; base decisions on her needs and the whole picture.

Recurrent self-harm is often a way of coping with unbearable feelings, but each episode is assessed on its own merits. “She always does this” misses rising risk; reflex admission or new sedatives can reinforce the crisis cycle. Decide the response from what she says today: intent, plan, means, and whether she can agree a plan.

CG78 [1]: do not use drug treatment specifically for borderline personality disorder or its individual symptoms. Short-term sedative medication may be considered cautiously in a crisis, for no longer than 1 week, with a drug that is relatively safe in overdose. NG225 [2]: do not offer drugs specifically to reduce self-harm. Treat comorbid depression or anxiety on their own terms.

Structured psychological therapy through the mental health service is the mainstay. CG78 [1] advises considering a comprehensive dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) programme for women for whom reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority, and advises against brief psychological interventions (under 3 months) for the disorder itself. QS88 [3] sets structured psychological therapy as a quality standard.

Idealisation (“you’re the only one who understands”) can flip to feeling abandoned. Consistent, kind limits, a predictable follow-up, and one plan shared with the team protect her better than open-ended promises. Offer a named clinician or regular appointments where the practice can sustain them.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let her speak first; stayed calm; acknowledged her distress and her courage in asking for help.
Relationship ending, being alone tonight, support network, what has helped before.
Picked up “I don’t know what I’ll do” and “everyone gives up on me” and explored both.
Idea (the GP can fix it now), concern (being abandoned), expectation (rescue today).
Recent self-harm: method, depth and wound care (checked on camera); suicidal thoughts, plans, preparation, means; protective factors.
Crisis in EUPD after a loss, versus a depressive episode or rising suicidal intent; asked without using a risk score.
Asked directly about suicide and means; decided on escalation from her answers, not from a label.
Linked her feelings to her known diagnosis without stigma; explained why therapy, not tablets, treats it.
Same-day crisis team referral with GP-to-team phone call; written safety plan; means reduction.
No reflex sedative or new drug in crisis (CG78, NG225); comorbid depression or anxiety to be assessed on its own terms.
Named crisis contacts, 999 or A&E if unsafe, GP call next day, and a regular appointment for continuity.

social.t: A relationship ending is a classic trigger for abandonment fear. She is alone tonight, so practical support, contact with the crisis team and a set call-back time matter.
People with this diagnosis often report being dismissed by services. A non-judgemental response in primary care makes it more likely she will ask for help next time instead of hurting herself.

legal.t: Assume capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005). She consents to the crisis referral here. If she refused help while at high immediate risk, capacity to make that decision would need assessing, and emergency services could be involved.
Sharing with the crisis team is part of her care and she agrees. If there were a serious and immediate risk to her life and she refused, GMC confidentiality guidance allows disclosure to protect her.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024) expects honest communication and continuity. A consistent plan shared with the team protects her better than an unsustainable special relationship with one GP.
Record what she said about intent, plans and means, the safety plan and the referral. Emotionally demanding consultations are a reason to use supervision or peer support, not to avoid the patient.

community.t: Local crisis resolution team, NHS 111 (mental health option in England), Samaritans 116 123, and local crisis cafés or safe havens where available. Mind has information for people with this diagnosis.

redFlags: Current suicidal intent or a plan, preparations or saved tablets
Escalating self-harm: deeper wounds, new methods, harm needing medical care
Alone, with access to means, and unable to agree a safety plan
Intoxication, or new psychotic or severe depressive symptoms
psychosocial: Relationship ending and being alone tonight
Her experience of services and fear of being given up on
ice: Idea: the GP can fix this now
Concern: being abandoned, as she feels everyone else has done

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “What you’re feeling now, the emptiness, the fear of people leaving, and cutting to make the pain stop, fits with the condition you already have. It’s a crisis, and crises pass, but you need proper support to get through this one safely.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Some people feel emotions much more intensely and for longer than others, like a volume dial stuck on high. When something painful happens, like a break-up, the feelings can become overwhelming. Therapy teaches ways to turn that dial down.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted me to fix it today. I can’t make the feelings disappear, but I can make sure you’re not facing tonight on your own and that help keeps going after today.”
management.psychosocial: She is alone after her partner left, so contact with the crisis team today, a GP call-back and a regular appointment give her structure.
sharedPlan: Same-day crisis team referral, with a GP phone call
Written safety plan: warning signs, her own coping strategies, people to contact, crisis numbers
No new sedative or other drug for the disorder; therapy (for example DBT) through the mental health team
Wound check on camera; face-to-face review if the cuts need care
safetyNet: Crisis team, NHS 111 mental health option or Samaritans 116 123 if distress rises
999 or A&E if she cannot keep herself safe
GP call tomorrow and a regular booked appointment

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by candidates who either rescue or reject. The marks go to a calm, warm consultation that asks directly about suicide, acts in proportion to what she says, and holds a kind boundary with a real plan.

items.fail: Never asking directly about suicidal thoughts, plans or means.
items.why: “I don’t know what I’ll do” is an ambiguous threat. Without direct questions the plan has no basis.
items.fix: “Are you having thoughts of ending your life? Any plan? Anything saved up or to hand?”

items.fail: Calling an ambulance or arranging admission as a reflex, or prescribing a sedative to end the call.
items.why: Over-reaction can reinforce the crisis cycle. CG78 advises against drug treatment for the disorder itself; NG225 advises against drugs to reduce self-harm.
items.fix: Decide from her answers. Here, same-day crisis team contact and a safety plan fit what she says.

items.fail: Assigning a “low risk” label and closing.
items.why: NG225 advises against low, medium or high risk labels to decide care.
items.fix: Base the plan on her needs: alone tonight, cut last night, passive suicidal thoughts.

items.fail: Promising to always be available, or agreeing that everyone else has failed her.
items.why: It feeds splitting and sets up the next abandonment.
items.fix: “I’ll stay involved, and I want a team around you too.”

items.fail: A cold boundary: “I can’t fix this, you need the mental health team.”
items.why: Limits without warmth feel like rejection to someone afraid of being dropped.
items.fix: Say what you can do today and when you will next speak.

items.fail: A vague safety-net: “ring if things get worse.”
items.why: She needs names, numbers and steps she can follow at 2 am.
items.fix: A written plan built from her own coping strategies, with crisis numbers, and teach-back.

items.why: Recent cuts may need care, and the video view is limited.
items.fix: Look on camera and arrange face-to-face review if needed.
